The first [mayor](/wiki/Mayor "Mayor") of [Philadelphia](/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") was [Humphrey Morrey](/wiki/Humphrey_Morrey "Humphrey Morrey"), who was appointed to the position by [William Penn](/wiki/William_Penn "William Penn"), the founder of the city and the colonial-era [Province of Pennsylvania](/wiki/Province_of_Pennsylvania "Province of Pennsylvania"), which became the state of Pennsylvania following the [American Revolutionary War](/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). Penn subsequently appointed [Edward Shippen](/wiki/Edward_Shippen "Edward Shippen") under the city charter of 1701. The [Philadelphia City Council](/wiki/Philadelphia_City_Council "Philadelphia City Council") then elected Shippen to a second term. Subsequent mayors, who held office for one year, were elected by the Philadelphia City Council. The initial mayors of Philadelphia were not compensated and candidates sometimes objected strongly to being selected to the position, sometimes choosing even to pay a fine rather than serve in the position.

In 1704, [alderman](/wiki/Alderman "Alderman") [Griffith Jones](/wiki/Griffith_Jones_(mayor) "Griffith Jones (mayor)") was elected but declined to serve, for which he was fined twenty pounds. In 1706, [Thomas Story](/wiki/Thomas_Story "Thomas Story"), also an alderman, was similarly fined for refusing office.

In 1745, Abraham Taylor, a Philadelphia alderman, was fined thirty pounds for refusing to assume the office. The city council then elected [Joseph Turner](/wiki/Joseph_Turner_(loyalist) "Joseph Turner (loyalist)"), who also refused and was likewise fined.[[2]](#cite_note-History-2) Others who refused election included [Richard Hill](/wiki/Richard_Hill_(Pennsylvania_politician) "Richard Hill (Pennsylvania politician)") (1717), [Issac Norris](/wiki/Isaac_Norris_(mayor) "Isaac Norris (mayor)") (1722), John Mifflin, and Alexander Stedman. Abhijit Banerjee was awarded the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in 2019 along with his two co-researchers [Esther Duflo](/wiki/Esther_Duflo "Esther Duflo") and [Michael Kremer](/wiki/Michael_Kremer "Michael Kremer") "for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty".[[39]](#cite_note-39)

The press release from the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") noted: "Their experimental research methods now entirely dominate [development economics](/wiki/Development_economics "Development economics")."[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-guardianlive-41)

The Nobel committee commented:

:   :   "Banerjee, Duflo and their co-authors concluded that students appeared to learn nothing from additional days at school. Neither did spending on textbooks seem to boost learning, even though the schools in [Kenya](/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") lacked many essential inputs. Moreover, in the Indian context Banerjee and Duflo intended to study, many children appeared to learn little: in results from field tests in the city of [Vadodara](/wiki/Vadodara "Vadodara") fewer than one in five third-grade students could correctly answer first-grade curriculum math test questions.[[41]](#cite_note-guardianlive-41)

:   :   "In response to such findings, Banerjee, Duflo and co-authors argued that efforts to get more children into school must be complemented by reforms to improve school quality."[[41]](#cite_note-guardianlive-41)

The Nobel Prize was a major recognition for their chosen field - Development Economics, and for the use of Randomised Controlled Trials. It evoked mixed emotions in India, where his success was celebrated with nationalistic fervour while his approach and pro-poor focus were seen as a negation of India's current government's right-wing ideology as well as broader development discourse.[[42]](#cite_note-42)

The non-Hispanic Black population of the city of Miami peaked in 1990 at almost 90,000, making up nearly a quarter of the population of Miami. Since then, Miami's non-Hispanic Black population has experienced a precipitous and steady decline. In the 2020 census, it was 52,447, only 11.7% of the population. Reasons for this include high costs in areas such as [Liberty City](/wiki/Liberty_City,_Miami "Liberty City, Miami") and [Little Haiti](/wiki/Little_Haiti "Little Haiti"), compounded with [gentrification](/wiki/Gentrification "Gentrification").[[89]](#cite_note-93)[[90]](#cite_note-94)

The non-Hispanic White population began to rebound in the twenty-first century, as the monolithically Hispanic areas in the Western and Central parts of Miami experienced population stagnation. This caused them to begin to be outweighed by migration into the Downtown region, from Latin America and the rest of the United States. This caused the non-Hispanic White population to rise from a nadir of 11.8% at the time of the [2000 census](/wiki/2000_United_States_census "2000 United States census") to 11.9% at the time of the [2010 census](/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census"). After this, the non-Hispanic White population grew significantly faster than Miami as a whole did during the 2010s. In the [2020 census](/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), non-Hispanic Whites were 14.0% of the population of Miami and numbered 61,829, the highest number since the 1980s. The non-Hispanic White population of Miami surpassed the non-Hispanic Black population of Miami in the 2010s.

Persian cat :: Breeding ethics :: chunk_0017
Persian cats, known for their facial structure, raise concerns about the ethics of breeding for certain deformities.

Brachycephaly is a highly sought-after characteristic producing big owl-like eyes and an overall petite-looking face. Though these features may be "cuter", they result in many health issues including ill-functioning [nasolacrimal ducts](/wiki/Nasolacrimal_duct "Nasolacrimal duct") where tears build and flow down the face, a soft and long palate that obstructs the upper airway making breathing more difficult, and dental and jaw defects ([brachygnathia](/wiki/Brachygnathia "Brachygnathia")) where the teeth grow outwardly in unnatural positions, making it difficult to eat and increasing the chance of plaque formation [gingivitis](/wiki/Gingivitis "Gingivitis").

Such health issues affect the quality of life of many Persian cats, especially those that fall into the severe category, and raise questions about the ethics and legality of these deformity breeding programmes. As a consequence of the [BBC](/wiki/BBC "BBC") programme *[Pedigree Dogs Exposed](/wiki/Pedigree_Dogs_Exposed "Pedigree Dogs Exposed")*, cat breeders have also come under pressure from veterinary and animal welfare associations, with the Persian singled out as one of the breeds most affected by health problems.[[88]](#cite_note-88) Animal welfare proponents have suggested changes to breed standards to prevent diseases caused by over- or ultra-typing, and prohibiting the breeding of animals outside the set limits.[[89]](#cite_note-89) Apart from the GCCF standard that limits high noses, TICA,[[23]](#cite_note-TICA_std-23) and FIFe standards require nostrils to be open, with FIFe stating that nostrils should allow "free and easy passage of air." Germany's Animal Welfare Act also prohibits the breeding of brachycephalic cats in which the tip of the nose is higher than the lower eyelids.[[67]](#cite_note-Schlueter-67)

**Jorge Mario Pedro Vargas Llosa,[[a]](#cite_note-1)[[b]](#cite_note-2) 1st Marquess of Vargas Llosa** (28 March 1936 – 13 April 2025) was a Peruvian novelist, journalist, essayist, and politician. Vargas Llosa was one of the most significant Latin American novelists and essayists and one of the leading writers of his generation. Some critics consider him to have had a more substantial international impact and worldwide audience than any other writer of the [Latin American Boom](/wiki/Latin_American_Boom "Latin American Boom"). [In 2010](/wiki/2010_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "2010 Nobel Prize in Literature"), he won the [Nobel Prize in Literature](/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature") for "his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual's resistance, revolt, and defeat".

Vargas Llosa rose to international fame in the 1960s with novels such as *[The Time of the Hero](/wiki/The_Time_of_the_Hero "The Time of the Hero")* (*La ciudad y los perros*, 1963/1966), *[The Green House](/wiki/The_Green_House "The Green House")* (*La casa verde*, 1965/1968), and the monumental *[Conversation in The Cathedral](/wiki/Conversation_in_The_Cathedral "Conversation in The Cathedral")* (*Conversación en La Catedral*, 1969/1975).[[c]](#cite_note-3) He wrote prolifically across various [literary genres](/wiki/Literary_genre "Literary genre"), including [literary criticism](/wiki/Literary_criticism "Literary criticism") and journalism. His novels include comedies, murder mysteries, historical novels, and political thrillers. He won the 1967 [Rómulo Gallegos Prize](/wiki/R%C3%B3mulo_Gallegos_Prize "Rómulo Gallegos Prize") and the 1986 [Prince of Asturias Award](/wiki/Prince_of_Asturias_Award "Prince of Asturias Award"). When combined with the Earth–Moon system's common orbit around the Sun, the period of the [synodic month](/wiki/Synodic_month "Synodic month"), from new moon to new moon, is 29.53 days.

Viewed from the [celestial north pole](/wiki/Celestial_pole "Celestial pole"), the motion of Earth, the Moon, and their axial rotations are all [counterclockwise](/wiki/Counterclockwise "Counterclockwise"). Viewed from Earth, the Moon is just far enough away to have almost the same apparent-sized disk as the Sun.
